sources.title: Battle of the Coral Sea, 4-8 May 1942: Summary

sections.title: Historical background
sections.text: After Pearl Harbor Japanese forces expanded rapidly across the Pacific and South-east Asia. By April 1942 Japan had established a defensive perimeter and sought to extend it.

sections.title: Political and strategic context
sections.text: Japan planned to advance south-east from the Bismarcks and Solomons and seize control of the Coral Sea between Australia and New Caledonia, establishing air bases at Port Moresby in New Guinea and Tulagi in the Solomons. Allied signals intelligence uncovered the plan to take Port Moresby, and all available Allied sea and air power was alerted.

sections.title: Campaign objectives
sections.text: The Japanese aimed to take Tulagi and then land at Port Moresby, with a carrier strike force to find and destroy the Allied naval forces that came to oppose them. The Allies aimed to stop the invasion of Port Moresby.

sections.title: Geography and terrain
sections.text: The battle was fought over the Coral Sea, between New Guinea, the Solomons and Australia. The opposing carrier forces searched for each other over wide areas of ocean, and their ships never came within sight of each other.

sections.title: Opposing forces and command structures
sections.text: Two US carrier task forces, built around Yorktown and Lexington under Rear Admiral Frank J. Fletcher, and a combined US–Australian cruiser force that included HMAS Australia and Hobart, faced the Japanese Carrier Strike Force with the fleet carriers Shōkaku and Zuikaku, supporting units and the invasion force from Rabaul, and the light carrier Shōhō.

sections.title: Initial deployment
sections.text: When the Japanese landed at Tulagi on 3 May, aircraft from Fletcher's task force struck the landing group on 4 May. The invasion force left Rabaul for Port Moresby, and its covering units took a route that invited a clash with Fletcher. The Allied cruisers were detached to guard against the Port Moresby invasion force.

sections.title: Chronological phases
sections.text: On 5 and 6 May the carrier groups searched for each other. On the morning of 7 May Japanese aircraft sank the destroyer Sims and the oiler Neosho, while Fletcher's aircraft sank the light carrier Shōhō and a cruiser. On 8 May both sides struck at each other's carriers: Japanese aircraft sank Lexington, which was abandoned after explosions and fires, and damaged Yorktown, while US aircraft damaged Shōkaku so badly that she had to retire. With its air cover weakened and under attack by Allied land-based bombers, the Port Moresby invasion force turned back to Rabaul.

sections.title: Important command decisions
sections.text: Acting on intelligence, the Allies committed their carriers to meet the Japanese advance. Both sides made many mistakes in the new kind of fighting; the Naval History and Heritage Command quotes Samuel Eliot Morison calling it a battle of errors in which the enemy made more and failed to profit by them. The Japanese decision to turn back the invasion force, once their air groups were too battered to cover it, decided the outcome.

sections.title: Decisive turning points
sections.text: The heavy losses of Japanese aircraft and the damage to Shōkaku left the Japanese unable to cover the landing at Port Moresby, and the invasion was called off.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.text: The Japanese sank more ships, and the Naval History and Heritage Command calls the battle a Japanese tactical victory. But Port Moresby remained in Allied hands, and Britannica calls the battle a strategic Allied victory. It was the first time since Pearl Harbor that the Japanese advance had been checked.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.text: Shōkaku was too badly damaged to join the force for Midway, and Zuikaku, having lost pilots and aircraft, did not take part either; Coral Sea reduced the carriers available to Japan for Midway by a third. It was the first naval battle in which the ships never sighted or fired at each other, and it foreshadowed the carrier warfare of the rest of the Pacific War.

sections.title: Historical lessons
sections.text: A tactical draw, or even a tactical defeat, can be a strategic victory if it stops the enemy's purpose. Intelligence that reveals the enemy's objective allows a weaker force to be in the right place. In carrier warfare, reconnaissance under uncertainty decides who strikes first and at what.

sections.title: Historiographical debates
sections.text: The sources judge the outcome differently: the Naval History and Heritage Command calls it a Japanese tactical victory that nonetheless stopped the advance, Britannica a strategic Allied victory. The Naval History and Heritage Command dates the operations from 29 April, Britannica and the Australian War Memorial the battle from 4 May.

sections.title: Source references
sections.text: The Naval History and Heritage Command gives the Japanese plan, the air strikes, the losses and the battle's effect on Midway. Britannica gives the intelligence, the course of the battle and its strategic result. The Australian War Memorial gives the Allied forces, including the Australian cruisers, and the turning back of the invasion force.
